So recall that a linear program is an optimization problem where you have some variables which
describe the quantities you want to compute and you now have linear constraints on these
variables as well as a linear function describing what it is that you want to optimize, maximize
or minimize.
That is called the objective function.
And one way to solve a linear program is to think of it geometrically and use the simplex
algorithm.
And the simplex algorithm exploits the fact that the optimum value of a linear program
is always at the vertex of the feasible region.
So it starts at some vertex and it keeps going from one vertex to a neighbor until it finds
a vertex whose value is optimum with respect to its neighbors and the claim is that that
vertex actually represents a solution.
You also said that we can justify that this is the optimum value by constructing the
dual which asks how to combine the constraints together to minimize the combination and the
solution which solves both the original and the dual is actually an optimum value.
So the next example we are going to look at is a carpet manufacturing company.

text: So let us now think of the constraints.
So the first constraint is the usual one which is that every quantity that we are talking
about is strictly greater than equal to 0.
The second constraint talks about how the number of carpets made break up into the regular
production for the overtime.
So if I make eye carpets in a month then each worker remember W I is a number of workers
in my establishment in Mantae will make 20.
So 20 times W I is what workers in Mantae produce in the normal time.
And in addition to that O I is just the number of carpets made.
Say O I is not the number of hours overtime.
So O I is the number of carpets.
So each month I make 20 times number of workers plus O I.
Now if I start if I had I minus 1 W I minus 1 workers last month and I hired a few
and I fired a few then the total number I have now is the old number plus the number
I have hired plus minus number I fired.
So this is a constraint on how each of the W I is connected to the previous W I.
Similarly the stock is connected to how much I had before I started this month.
How much I made this month and how much I sold.
So remember that D1 to D12 was the demand.
So this is a fixed quantity these are not variables these are known values.
So in this month I would have sold D I but I produced XI.
So XI minus D I is the excess that I produced this month or the deficit as the case may
be.
I started with a surplus of XI minus 1.
So if I add this month's surplus or defile I get the total surplus at the end of the
month.
And remember I cannot have negative content.
So XI all these things must always be bigger than equal to 0.
And finally as we said before a worker who produces 20 copies in a regular month if I
add now the fact that he can do 30 percent overtime.
This is 20 plus 6.
So the number of copies made in overtime can be at most 6 per worker.
So OI should be less than or equal to 6 times W I.
So these are our constraints now.
So now given these constraints what we want to do is minimize the total amount of costs
that we are going to put out.
So first this is the regular salary cost.
Yes the regular salary cost is 20,000 per worker and we have W1 workers in month 1, W2
and month 2 and W2 are in month 12.
So we add up the total number of workers each of them is 20,000 rupees.
So this is our total salary bill for the year.
Then depending on how many people we hire in each month for each hire we pay 3000.
So this is our hiring bill.
Similarly for each person that we dismiss we have to pay 4000 first that.
So this is our firing bill.
Then the number of copies that we have to keep in storage in each month in person 80 rupees
per carpet cost.
So I have to multiply the total storage by 80.
And finally when I pay overtime I am paying over and above the salary.
So each carpet made in overtime remember cost 1800 rupees as opposed to 1000 rupees which
is already accounted for in the salary.
So this is my overtime cost.
So now so this says that we can take this fairly complicated looking question about production
with demand and hiring and firing and productivity and all that and set it up with some 72 plus
274 variables and a complex cost function and feed it to simplex and get an answer.
So we run simplex and we find a solution.
So are we done?
So it turns out that we might get an answer which is not something that we can actually
use.
For instance we might get an answer which says age 3 is equal to 10.6.
So this says that we must hire a fractional number of people in a month.
Now obviously we cannot do this.
At the same time we have not in any of our constraints express that the values must be
integers.
So what can we do about this?
Well we can take this 10.6 and we can look for the nearest integer 10 or 11 and re-evaluate
what happens to the cost if we make it to an integer.
This is called integer rounding.
Now if the values are big, they like 10, 11 if they are two digit values say then rounding
is a relatively small displacement and the quality of the optimum will not change much
based on this.
But if the numbers are small if I am rounding between say I am going to take it from 0.5
to 1 or 0 or from 1.5 to 2 or 1 then the effect of that rounding can be quite trust.
So this is a general problem with linear programming which is linear programming cannot
guarantee you that you have integer solutions when you want an integer solution.
You can use a rounding to achieve an integer solution but you have to be careful that the
rounding actually gives you an optimum.
Now why not just insist that you want an integer solution.
So can you not set up the same problem and solve it but require the solutions to be
integers.
Unfortunately this turns out to be quite a hard problem.
So we have found we have claimed rather that when we set up general linear programming
problems we can solve them efficiently.
So simplex is not an efficient solution but an effective solution but there are interior
point methods and other polynomial time algorithms called linear programming.
But if we change the rules of the game and say I do not want an arbitrary solution that
meets the constraints but I want to one where all the values that I get are integers then
we have the so called integer linear programming problem.
An integer linear programming unfortunately is not solvable efficiently or at least not
known to be solvable efficiently.
So the best we can hope to do for integer linear programming is to actually try to turn
it into an arbitrary linear program and somehow interpret the answers as integers by doing
appropriate rounding.
